name: Cista++
workload: Serialize/deserialize/traverse a pointer-based object-oriented graph (nodes + edges, indices instead of raw pointers) via Google Benchmark on an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (GCC 11, Ubuntu 20.04, cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release)
claimed_speedup: Combined deserialize+traverse: Cista++ 'offset' variant 66ms vs cereal 174ms (~2.6x faster, most representative apples-to-apples figure). Component legs show much larger gaps that reflect Cista's zero-copy in-place layout rather than a faster general parser: serialize 4ms vs cereal's 216ms (~54x), deserialize 0.16ms vs cereal's 111.00ms (~694x, essentially free because no parsing step is needed).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11, cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (exact -O flag not printed in README; no DEBUG/-O0 involved)
tradeoffs: Zero-copy 'offset' format is not portable across pointer-width/endianness without extra care, requires structs to be layout-describable to Cista's reflection (aggregate-like), and the very low deserialize cost is an architectural artifact (buffer is used in place) rather than a faster decoder; the non-zero-copy 'raw' variant is much slower to serialize (650ms, slower than cereal's 216ms) though still faster to deserialize (24.8ms vs 111ms).
caveats: cereal is the only one of the two assignment baselines present in this specific benchmark suite (no Boost.Serialization comparison here); this repo (felixguendling/cpp-serialization-benchmark) is not itself the Cista repo but its author's companion benchmark for it. The >50x figures for serialize/deserialize legs would normally trigger a tier cap per the implausible-ratio rule, but they are explained by Cista's documented zero-copy design (identical to how Cap'n Proto shows near-0ms deserialize in the same suite), not a measurement artifact; the combined deserialize+traverse number (2.6x) is offered as the fair comparison. Cista itself is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST); reported here only as new Tier B evidence for it beating a named baseline.

name: zpp_bits
workload: Serialize/deserialize a 'Monster' struct (Vec3 pos, mana/hp, name, inventory vector<uint8_t>, Color enum, vector<Weapon>, equipped Weapon, vector<Vec3> path) for 50 monsters, 300000 iterations ('general' test case), on Ubuntu 20.04 x64
claimed_speedup: GCC 11: zpp_bits 733ms serialize / 693ms deserialize vs Boost.Serialization 15126ms / 12724ms (~20.6x / ~18.4x faster) and vs cereal 10777ms / 9088ms (~14.7x / ~13.1x faster). Clang 12.0.1: zpp_bits 790ms/715ms vs Boost 16011ms/13017ms (~20.3x/~18.2x) and vs cereal 9977ms/8565ms (~12.6x/~12.0x).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1 on Ubuntu 20.04 x64 via plain `cmake .. && make` (no explicit -O flag printed, not a DEBUG build)
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04 x64 (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Uses C++20 structured-binding-based reflection ('visit_members' style) so it needs no macros or codegen step, but relies on aggregate-friendly types and header-only compile-time machinery that can increase compile times; format is a compact, non-self-describing binary layout (less forward/backward-compatible out of the box than Boost.Serialization's versioning or cereal's named-field JSON archives).
caveats: Tier B rather than A because the exact CPU model and literal compiler optimization flags are not printed in the README (only 'Ubuntu 20.04 x64' and a plain cmake build); numbers come from the benchmark author (fraillt, also author of the competing 'bitsery' library, itself in KNOWN_LIST), which is disclosed as a potential source of author bias though the harness and methodology are open and reproducible. zpp_bits is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST); reported here only as new Tier B evidence for it beating both named baselines directly with a common methodology.
found_via: WebSearch: 'CppCon static reflection serialization performance faster than cereal' -> led to felixguendling/cpp-serialization-benchmark 'Other Benchmarks' links -> github.com/fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark (opened via gh api repos/fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark/contents/README.md)

name: FlatBuffers
workload: Same 'Monster' struct benchmark as above (schema-compiled via flatc codegen instead of reflection), 300000 iterations, Ubuntu 20.04 x64
claimed_speedup: GCC 11: FlatBuffers 8757ms serialize / 3361ms deserialize vs Boost.Serialization 15126ms/12724ms (~1.7x/~3.8x faster) and vs cereal 10777ms/9088ms (~1.2x/~2.7x faster). Clang 12.0.1: 9812ms/3472ms vs Boost 16011ms/13017ms and cereal 9977ms/8565ms (similar ratios).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1 on Ubuntu 20.04 x64 via plain `cmake .. && make` (no explicit -O flag printed)
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04 x64 (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires a schema (.fbs) and a codegen step (flatc) rather than reflecting existing C++ types directly, so it needs adapter/conversion code when the wire schema differs from the application's own structs (which the benchmark author explicitly flags as adding overhead in this specific test); in exchange it gives true zero-copy random access to serialized buffers.
caveats: The benchmark README itself notes: 'tests for protobuf and flatbuffers is not 100% fair, because huge amount of CPU cycles goes to converting from generated types to our defined types' -- so the reported numbers likely understate FlatBuffers' raw advantage. FlatBuffers is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST) as a general fast-serialization entry; reported here only as new Tier B evidence that it beats both Boost.Serialization and cereal specifically, using schema-driven codegen (the 'codegen' half of this category) rather than compile-time reflection.
found_via: Same fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark page as zpp_bits entry above

name: Cap'n Proto
workload: 1,000,000 serialize+deserialize operations of a fixed schema-compiled test message, averaged over 50 runs, on 'a typical desktop computer with Intel Core i7 processor' running Ubuntu 16.04
claimed_speedup: Cap'n Proto avg total time 400.98ms vs Boost.Serialization 1195.04ms (~2.98x faster) and vs cereal 1052.46ms (~2.62x faster).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated precisely for the published numbers (README: 'tested with Clang and GCC compilers', built via cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; which compiler produced the table is unspecified)
hardware: 'typical desktop computer with Intel Core i7 processor', Ubuntu 16.04 (exact CPU model/generation not given)
tradeoffs: Requires a .capnp schema and codegen step; for Cap'n Proto and FlatBuffers the README explicitly notes the measured cycle is build+serialize+deserialize (since the wire format doubles as the in-memory representation) whereas the other libraries in the same table only measure serialize/deserialize of an already-built structure, so the comparison is not perfectly apples-to-apples.
caveats: Evidence tier capped at B: exact compiler and CPU model are not stated for the published run, only 'GCC and Clang' generically and a generic 'Intel Core i7'. Cap'n Proto is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST); reported here only as new Tier B evidence that it beats both named baselines on a public, versioned (thrift 0.12.0/boost 1.69.0/cereal 1.2.2/etc.) benchmark.

name: reflect-cpp
workload: No quantified workload against Boost.Serialization/cereal was found; reflect-cpp's own quantified benchmarks (canada/licenses/person structs, GCC 11.4, Ubuntu 22.04) compare only its JSON/msgpack/flexbuffers/cbor/bson/xml/toml/yaml backends against each other and against RapidJSON/nlohmann::json, not against Boost.Serialization or cereal.
claimed_speedup: Unquantified: README states reflect-cpp is 'one of the fastest serialization libraries in existence, as demonstrated by our benchmarks' and (for JSON only, not our baselines) 'faster than RapidJSON, usually about twice as fast' and 'consistently about 10 times faster than nlohmann/json'. No number appears anywhere comparing reflect-cpp's rfl::boost_serialization or rfl::cereal backends' speed to using Boost.Serialization/cereal directly, even though the benchmark source (benchmarks/all/person_write.cpp etc.) defines BM_person_write_reflect_cpp_boost_serialization and BM_person_write_reflect_cpp_cereal functions -- the published chart images (benchmarks/img/*.png) omit those two formats entirely.
tradeoffs: Because rfl::boost_serialization and rfl::cereal are thin reflection-generated glue layers over the real upstream Boost.Serialization and Cereal libraries (not reimplementations), reflect-cpp cannot outrun those two backends' own serialization speed -- its actual value proposition versus them is eliminating hand-written serialize()/save()/load() boilerplate (one line of code vs the intrusive-function pattern both baselines require), not raw throughput. Its genuine speed wins (vs RapidJSON/nlohmann::json, and its own msgpack/flexbuffers backends beating its own cereal/boost backends in the source-level benchmark suite, per unreleased chart data) are against non-baseline targets.
caveats: Tier D by rule (notable project, >1k stars, but no numbers for the specific named baselines). Included because it is the clearest example found of a C++ reflection-and-codegen library explicitly designed to interoperate with both Boost.Serialization and cereal as pluggable backends (rfl.hpp / rfl/boost_serialization.hpp / rfl/cereal.hpp), which is exactly this category's subject, even though no head-to-head speed number against them could be verified this session.
